patient.name: Tomasz Nowak
patient.complaint: Called back about a very high cholesterol on routine bloods; feels well
background: Father died of a heart attack aged 48

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis/cause?' with a very high cholesterol plus tendon xanthomas and a premature family history (familial hypercholesterolaemia), or a secondary cause hidden in the stem (hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, diabetes).

points: He smokes and eats takeaways most days.

steps.lead: Like most people with high lipids, Tomasz has **no symptoms**: it was found on routine bloods.

points: On examination: firm **lumps in both Achilles tendons**.
Yellow plaques on both upper eyelids.

steps.lead: Tomasz has both classic signs: **xanthelasma** on his eyelids and **tendon xanthomas** on his Achilles.
Very high cholesterol plus **tendon xanthomas** plus a father with an early MI: this is **familial hypercholesterolaemia** until proven otherwise.

visual.title: Total cholesterol
visual.label: Tomasz 9.2
visual.caption: Above **7.5 mmol/L** should prompt investigation for familial hypercholesterolaemia.

steps.lead: FH is the **primary** cause here; secondary causes such as diabetes, **hypothyroidism** and obesity still need excluding.

steps.q: Which secondary cause of high cholesterol is reversible and must be checked in Tomasz?
steps.r: **Hypothyroidism** is a reversible cause of hypercholesterolaemia, so TFTs are checked before a statin.

steps.lead: Tomasz has no oedema, but **nephrotic syndrome** is another secondary cause: protein loss drives the liver to make more lipoprotein.
Tomasz's real danger is **accelerated atherosclerosis**: his father's early MI shows what untreated FH can do.

steps.text: Xanthelasma alone is common and often has **normal** lipids. Tendon xanthomas are the sign that points to FH.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' for a full lipid profile, QRISK3 for primary prevention, TFTs/LFTs/HbA1c before a statin, and the total cholesterol/HDL ratio as the best predictor of risk.

steps.title: Tomasz's fasting lipid profile
steps.text: Very high LDL with **normal triglycerides**: the classic FH pattern.

steps.lead: Tomasz's **full lipid profile** confirms it; his **TC/HDL ratio of 8.4** is the best single predictor of his cardiovascular risk.

steps.q: Which lipid measure best predicts Tomasz's cardiovascular risk?
steps.r: The **TC/HDL ratio** is the best predictor. LDL is the **treatment target**.

steps.lead: Most people get a **QRISK3** score; Tomasz's total cholesterol over **7.5** sends him down the FH route instead.

visual.title: QRISK3 10-year CVD risk (primary prevention)
visual.label: Tomasz's brother 12%
visual.caption: For a typical patient, **QRISK3 ≥10%** means offer atorvastatin 20 mg. QRISK3 underestimates risk in FH.

steps.title: Secondary causes and pre-statin bloods
steps.text: No hypothyroidism, diabetes or liver disease: no secondary cause, and safe to start a statin.

steps.lead: Tomasz has **HbA1c, TFTs and LFTs** before treatment, and will repeat lipids and LFTs at **3 months**.

steps.text: Do not start a statin without checking **TFTs**: treating undiagnosed hypothyroidism may fix the cholesterol and avoid statin myopathy.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' choosing the statin dose: atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention (QRISK3 ≥10%), 80 mg for established CVD, high-intensity plus lipid clinic for FH, then ezetimibe.

steps.q: Tomasz has likely FH. What is the most appropriate management?
o: High-intensity statin and lipid clinic referral
steps.r: In FH, start a **high-intensity statin promptly** and **refer to a lipid specialist** (with family cascade testing).

steps.lead: Everyone starts with **lifestyle**: Tomasz is advised to stop smoking, cut saturated fat and exercise. A **statin** is the first drug.
Because Tomasz has **FH**, he goes straight onto **high-intensity** atorvastatin and is referred to the **lipid clinic**.

visual.title: Tomasz's non-HDL cholesterol
visual.caption: Statin alone gave a 31% fall: below the **40%** target, so **ezetimibe** was added.

steps.lead: At **3 months** Tomasz's non-HDL had fallen by only 31%, so **ezetimibe** was added; **PCSK9 inhibitors** come after that.
Tomasz's plan follows **NICE CG181**; QRISK3 and Framingham are used for people without FH.

steps.text: Statins are **contraindicated in pregnancy**. Ask about muscle aches; check **CK** only if he develops muscle symptoms.
Numbers to know: **20 mg** primary, **80 mg** secondary, review at **3 months**, aim for **>40%** non-HDL reduction.

science.exam: Expect applied questions on the mechanism of statins (HMG-CoA reductase), the defect in FH (LDL receptor, autosomal dominant) and why hypothyroidism or nephrotic syndrome raise cholesterol.

steps.lead: Tomasz's excess **LDL** is being deposited in his artery walls; his **HDL** works the other way, returning cholesterol to the liver.

steps.title: From LDL to plaque
nodes: LDL enters the arterial intima and is oxidised
Fatty streak grows into a plaque

steps.lead: Tomasz probably carries an **autosomal dominant LDL receptor** mutation: his liver cannot clear LDL, so it has been high since birth.

steps.q: Tomasz's father had FH. What is the chance each of Tomasz's children inherits it?
steps.r: **Autosomal dominant**: each child of one affected parent has a **50%** chance. This is why cascade testing matters.

steps.lead: Tomasz's atorvastatin blocks **HMG-CoA reductase**, so his liver cells make more **LDL receptors** and pull LDL out of the blood.

steps.title: How a statin lowers LDL
nodes: Less cholesterol made in the hepatocyte

steps.lead: Tomasz's normal TSH rules out the **hypothyroid** mechanism; nephrotic syndrome would act through **hepatic lipoprotein synthesis**.

mcq.q: Which sign most strongly suggests familial hypercholesterolaemia?
mcq.r: Very high cholesterol plus **tendon xanthomas** strongly suggests FH.

mcq.q: Which is a reversible secondary cause of hypercholesterolaemia?
mcq.r: **Hypothyroidism** reduces LDL receptor expression; treating it lowers cholesterol.

mcq.q: What is the key complication of hyperlipidaemia?
mcq.r: **Cardiovascular disease** (IHD and stroke) from accelerated atherosclerosis.

mcq.q: What is the best lipid predictor of cardiovascular risk?
mcq.r: The **TC/HDL ratio**; LDL is the treatment target.

mcq.q: Which total cholesterol should prompt investigation for FH?
Which tests are done before starting a statin?
mcq.r: **LFTs, full lipid profile and TFTs**; repeat lipids and LFTs at 3 months.

mcq.q: Which statin is used for primary prevention when QRISK3 is ≥10%?
Which statin is used for secondary prevention?
mcq.r: **High-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg** regardless of baseline lipids.

mcq.q: What is added first if a statin alone is not enough?
mcq.r: **Ezetimibe** first; PCSK9 inhibitors are reserved for escalation.
**HMG-CoA reductase**, the rate-limiting step of hepatic cholesterol synthesis.

technique.stem: A 35 year old man has a routine health check. He has no symptoms. His father died of a myocardial infarction aged 46. There are firm nodules over both Achilles tendons. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question with a lipid profile: primary or secondary, and which pattern?

clues: father died of a myocardial infarction aged 46
firm nodules over both Achilles tendons
steps.x: Premature family CVD, **tendon xanthomas**, very high LDL with normal triglycerides.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Familial hypercholesterolaemia**.

elim: Familial combined hyperlipidaemia raises **triglycerides** too and does not cause tendon xanthomas.
TSH is normal.
No oedema or proteinuria is described.
Rheumatoid nodules sit on extensor surfaces with joint disease.

steps.x: **B. Familial hypercholesterolaemia.** Rule: very high cholesterol + tendon xanthomas + early family MI = FH.

technique.stem: A 52 year old woman has a fasting lipid profile at her GP. She asks which number best tells her how likely she is to have a heart attack or stroke. She has no history of cardiovascular disease.
technique.q: Which is the best predictor of her cardiovascular risk from this lipid profile?

steps.x: Best **predictor of risk** from the lipid profile, not the treatment target.
Risk prediction for primary prevention.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **total cholesterol/HDL ratio**.

elim: HDL alone ignores the atherogenic lipids.
LDL is the **treatment target**, not the best predictor.
Total cholesterol alone ignores protective HDL.
Triglycerides are a weaker independent predictor.

steps.x: **D. Total cholesterol/HDL ratio.** Rule: ratio predicts, LDL is targeted.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman has a total cholesterol of 9.8 mmol/L and LDL cholesterol of 7.9 mmol/L. She has tendon xanthomas on her knuckles and her mother had a myocardial infarction aged 50. Her TSH, HbA1c and LFTs are normal. She is not pregnant and is using contraception. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Atorvastatin 20 mg and repeat lipids in 1 year
High-intensity statin and referral to a lipid specialist

steps.x: Management: decide primary prevention, secondary prevention or FH.

clues: mother had a myocardial infarction aged 50
steps.x: Clinical **FH**; secondary causes excluded; statin is safe.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Start a **high-intensity statin promptly** and **refer to a lipid specialist**.

elim: 20 mg is the QRISK3 primary-prevention dose; FH needs high intensity and specialist care.
Ezetimibe is added to a statin, not used first.
Lifestyle alone is not enough in FH.
PCSK9 inhibitors are reserved for escalation.

steps.x: **C. High-intensity statin and lipid specialist referral.** Rule: FH = do not use QRISK3; treat high and refer.

technique.stem: A 60 year old man starts atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention. Three months later his LDL cholesterol has fallen from 4.6 to 2.3 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the fall in plasma LDL?
o: Reduced hepatic VLDL secretion via PPAR-alpha

steps.x: Mechanism of a **statin** on plasma LDL.
A statin; LDL roughly halved.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HMG-CoA reductase blocked → less intracellular cholesterol → **more LDL receptors** → more LDL cleared.

elim: Fibrates act via lipoprotein lipase and PPAR-alpha.
That is **ezetimibe**.
That is a **PCSK9 inhibitor**.
That describes fibrates.

steps.x: **E. Upregulation of hepatic LDL receptors.** Rule: statin blocks synthesis, receptors rise, plasma LDL falls.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has a routine health check. She is asymptomatic. Her brother had a myocardial infarction aged 44. She has thickened Achilles tendons with firm nodules. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Very high LDL with normal triglycerides, tendon xanthomas and a premature family MI is familial hypercholesterolaemia. Combined and hypertriglyceridaemic forms raise triglycerides.

steps.x: Diagnosis from a lipid pattern plus examination.

clues: brother had a myocardial infarction aged 44
thickened Achilles tendons with firm nodules
steps.x: Early family CVD and **tendon xanthomas**; LDL very high, TG normal, TSH normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Familial hypercholesterolaemia**.

elim: Combined hyperlipidaemia raises triglycerides too.
Triglycerides are normal.
TSH is normal.
Obesity does not cause tendon xanthomas or LDL of 8.

steps.x: **B. Familial hypercholesterolaemia.** Rule: tendon xanthomas + very high LDL + normal TG = FH.

practice.stem: A 54 year old woman has a 6 month history of tiredness, weight gain, constipation and feeling cold. Her skin is dry and her reflexes are slow-relaxing. Her pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg. A routine lipid profile shows raised cholesterol.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypercholesterolaemia?
practice.e: Tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, bradycardia and slow-relaxing reflexes point to hypothyroidism, a reversible secondary cause of hypercholesterolaemia. Normal HbA1c and no proteinuria exclude diabetes and nephrotic syndrome.

steps.x: The **cause** of high cholesterol: look for a secondary cause in the history.

clues: tiredness, weight gain, constipation and feeling cold
steps.x: Classic hypothyroid features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hypothyroidism**: reduced LDL receptors and lipoprotein lipase activity.

elim: No tendon xanthomas or family history; cholesterol only moderately raised.
Urine protein is negative.
Weight gain is a symptom here, not the root cause.
HbA1c is normal.

steps.x: **B. Hypothyroidism.** Rule: always check TFTs; it is a reversible cause.

practice.stem: A 6 year old boy has a 2 week history of puffy eyes and swollen legs. His urine is frothy. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. There is periorbital and pitting leg oedema. A lipid profile is markedly abnormal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hyperlipidaemia?
practice.e: Oedema, heavy proteinuria and low albumin are nephrotic syndrome, which causes hyperlipidaemia as the liver increases lipoprotein synthesis in response to low oncotic pressure.

steps.x: The cause of the lipids: look at what else is going on.
Oedema, proteinuria (PCR 620) and albumin 18: **nephrotic syndrome**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Nephrotic syndrome** driving hepatic lipoprotein synthesis.

elim: FH does not cause oedema or proteinuria.
TSH is normal.
Nothing suggests obesity.
No polyuria, weight loss or hyperglycaemia.

steps.x: **C. Nephrotic syndrome.** Rule: oedema + proteinuria + low albumin + high lipids = nephrotic.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man has a total cholesterol of 9.8 mmol/L with normal triglycerides. His father died suddenly aged 49. He has no symptoms. His pulse rate is 66 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: Very high cholesterol with normal triglycerides and a premature family death suggests familial hypercholesterolaemia, which classically causes tendon xanthomas. Eruptive xanthomas and lipaemia retinalis come with very high triglycerides.

steps.x: An examination finding: first decide which lipid disorder.
High cholesterol, normal TG, early family death: **FH**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Tendon xanthomas** (Achilles, knuckles).

elim: Eruptive xanthomas need very high **triglycerides**.
Janeway lesions are infective endocarditis.
Lipaemia retinalis also needs very high triglycerides.
Spider naevi suggest chronic liver disease.

steps.x: **E. Tendon xanthomas.** Rule: high cholesterol = tendon xanthomas; high TG = eruptive.

practice.stem: A 48 year old man with familial hypercholesterolaemia stopped his statin 5 years ago because he felt well. He has not attended follow-up. His triglycerides have always been normal. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 146/90 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication he will develop?
practice.e: The key complication of hyperlipidaemia, especially FH, is cardiovascular disease from accelerated atherosclerosis. Pancreatitis complicates very high triglycerides, which he does not have.

steps.x: The most likely complication of untreated hypercholesterolaemia.
Untreated very high LDL plus smoking and hypertension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ischaemic heart disease** (or stroke) from atherosclerosis.

elim: Pancreatitis needs very high **triglycerides**.
NAFLD is linked to obesity and insulin resistance.
Not a complication of hyperlipidaemia.
Not linked to hypercholesterolaemia.

steps.x: **B. Ischaemic heart disease.** Rule: high LDL = atherosclerosis = IHD and stroke.

practice.stem: A 56 year old woman has noticed soft, flat yellow plaques on the inner corners of both upper eyelids over the past year. They are painless and not itchy. She is overweight and has type 2 diabetes. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her eyelid lesions?
practice.e: Soft, flat yellow plaques at the inner eyelids are xanthelasma, a classic sign of hyperlipidaemia; her diabetes and obesity are secondary causes.

steps.x: Name the cause of the eyelid lesions.

clues: inner corners of both upper eyelids
steps.x: Bilateral yellow plaques = **xanthelasma**; secondary causes present.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Xanthelasma from **hyperlipidaemia**.

elim: BCC is a pearly nodule, usually single, with rolled edges.
A chalazion is a firm lump within the lid, not a flat plaque.
Molluscum is umbilicated papules.
A cyst is a dome-shaped lump, not a flat yellow plaque.

steps.x: **C. Hyperlipidaemia.** Rule: yellow eyelid plaques = xanthelasma = check lipids.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with no cardiovascular disease has a QRISK3 score of 16%. He agrees to start a statin. He drinks 30 units of alcohol a week. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting treatment?
practice.e: Before starting a statin, check LFTs (with a full lipid profile and TFTs), then repeat lipids and LFTs at 3 months. CK is only checked if there are muscle symptoms.

steps.x: A **pre-statin** test.
Statins can raise transaminases; his alcohol makes liver disease more likely.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **LFTs** (plus lipid profile and TFTs).

elim: CK only if he has muscle pain.
He has no symptoms of angina.
No renal concern.
Urate is not needed for a statin.

steps.x: **C. Liver function tests.** Rule: before a statin = LFTs, lipids, TFTs; repeat at 3 months.

practice.stem: A 57 year old man had a myocardial infarction 4 months ago. He takes atorvastatin 80 mg and reports no side effects. He takes every dose. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. His lipids are repeated at 3 months.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman is diagnosed with familial hypercholesterolaemia. Her LDL cholesterol is 7.8 mmol/L with normal triglycerides. Her father and her sister are also affected. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying defect?
practice.e: FH is most commonly due to autosomal dominant mutations in the LDL receptor gene, which impair hepatic clearance of LDL. Apo C-II and lipoprotein lipase defects raise triglycerides; PCSK9 loss of function lowers LDL.

steps.x: The molecular defect in FH.

clues: Her father and her sister are also affected
steps.x: Isolated high LDL; vertical transmission suggests **autosomal dominant**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **LDL receptor gene** mutation: the liver cannot clear LDL.

elim: Apo C-II deficiency gives very high triglycerides.
Not the cause of FH.
Lipoprotein lipase deficiency also gives high triglycerides.
PCSK9 **loss** of function lowers LDL; gain of function is the rare FH cause.

steps.x: **C. LDL receptor gene mutation.** Rule: FH = autosomal dominant LDL receptor defect.

glossary.LDL: Low-density lipoprotein; carries cholesterol to tissues and deposits it in artery walls.
glossary.HDL: High-density lipoprotein; carries cholesterol back to the liver, protecting against atherosclerosis.
glossary.Non-HDL cholesterol: Total cholesterol minus HDL; the value NICE uses to judge statin response.
glossary.Triglycerides: Blood fats from diet and the liver; very high levels risk pancreatitis.
glossary.Lipid profile: Blood test measuring total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides.
glossary.Familial hypercholesterolaemia: Inherited, usually autosomal dominant, LDL receptor defect causing very high LDL from birth.
glossary.Xanthelasma: Soft yellow cholesterol plaques on the eyelids.
glossary.Tendon xanthomas: Cholesterol deposits in tendons such as the Achilles or knuckles; a hallmark of FH.
glossary.Eruptive xanthomas: Crops of small yellow papules on buttocks or limbs, seen with very high triglycerides.
glossary.Atherosclerosis: Build-up of fatty plaques in artery walls that narrow and can rupture.
glossary.Foam cell: Macrophage stuffed with oxidised LDL; the building block of a fatty streak.
glossary.Reverse cholesterol transport: HDL carrying cholesterol from tissues back to the liver for removal.
glossary.QRISK3: NICE-recommended score estimating 10-year risk of heart attack or stroke.
glossary.Framingham: An older cardiovascular risk score, an alternative to QRISK3.
glossary.Primary prevention: Treatment to prevent a first cardiovascular event in someone without CVD.
glossary.Secondary prevention: Treatment to prevent further events in someone with established CVD.
glossary.Statin: Drug that inhibits HMG-CoA reductase to lower LDL cholesterol.
glossary.Atorvastatin: Statin used at 20 mg for primary and 80 mg for secondary prevention.
glossary.HMG-CoA reductase: Rate-limiting enzyme in liver cholesterol synthesis; the target of statins.
glossary.LDL receptor: Liver cell receptor that removes LDL from the blood; defective in FH.
glossary.Ezetimibe: Blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption; first add-on when a statin is not enough.
glossary.PCSK9 inhibitor: Injectable antibody that stops LDL receptor breakdown; reserved for escalation.
glossary.PCSK9: Liver protein that destroys LDL receptors; gain-of-function mutations cause rare FH.
glossary.Autosomal dominant: Inheritance where one faulty copy causes disease; each child has a 50% risk.
glossary.Cascade testing: Testing the relatives of someone with an inherited condition such as FH.
glossary.Hypothyroidism: Underactive thyroid; a reversible cause of raised cholesterol.
glossary.TFTs: Thyroid function tests (TSH and free T4).
glossary.TSH: Thyroid-stimulating hormone; raised in primary hypothyroidism.
glossary.LFTs: Liver function tests; checked before and 3 months after starting a statin.
glossary.Nephrotic syndrome: Heavy proteinuria, low albumin and oedema, with raised lipids.
glossary.Oncotic pressure: Pull of plasma proteins (mainly albumin) that keeps fluid in vessels.
glossary.Lipoprotein lipase: Enzyme on vessel walls that breaks down triglyceride-rich lipoproteins.
glossary.CK: Creatine kinase; muscle enzyme checked if a patient on a statin has muscle pain.
glossary.IHD: Ischaemic heart disease: angina and myocardial infarction from coronary atherosclerosis.
glossary.NHS Health Check: Routine cardiovascular risk check for adults aged 40 to 74 in England.
